RAII stands for resource acquisition is initialisation, which is an awkward name for a plain idea: an object takes charge of a resource when it is created and gives it back when it is destroyed. The resource is anything you have to hand back. Heap memory, an open file, a socket, a lock, a ROS subscription.

The problem it solves is the cleanup you forget. You open a file at the top of a function and close it at the bottom, and then someone adds an early return in the middle, or a line between them throws, and the file stays open. Every exit path needs its own cleanup and the compiler cannot tell you which one you missed. RAII moves the cleanup into a destructor, and the language already promises to run that destructor when the object goes out of scope: on a return, on a break, and while an exception unwinds the stack. One place, every path.
That is why C++ has no
block. The destructor is the finally block, and it belongs to the resource rather than to whichever function happens to use it.

What it costs you is that the owner has to answer three questions the compiler would otherwise answer badly. Can it be copied, which usually means no, because two owners would each release the same handle. Can it be moved, which usually means yes, and the moved-from object has to be left safe to destroy.
